abstract: The ability to invent novel behavioral solutions was a crucial factor in the success of Homo species. Beyond humans, high levels of innovation have evolved independently across several animal lineages, including birds. Birds provide a particularly striking example, with highly innovative species distributed across multiple clades, creating an opportunity to investigate whether independent origins of this phenotype involve recurring evolutionary mechanisms. To investigate the genomic basis of avian innovativeness, we analyzed high-quality long-read genomes from a broad sampling of avian species, leveraging recent genomic resources from the Vertebrate Genomes Project. To investigate both lineage-specific molecular changes and broader genomic correlates of innovativeness, we analyzed coding sequences in selected clades where highly innovative species occur among less innovative relatives, and examined the evolutionary rates of conserved non-exonic elements (CNEEs) across the avian phylogeny using innovation as a continuous trait. We identified candidate genes under recurrent positive selection, including those implicated in neural development and function, as well as maternal nutrient provisioning to developing embryos. In parallel, CNEEs overlapping differentially accessible regions in glial cells and specific glutamatergic neuronal population of the avian pallium showed stronger evolutionary constraint in more innovative lineages. Together, these findings link the evolution of avian innovativeness across distinct branches of the avian phylogeny to molecular changes spanning neural function, early developmental processes, and the regulation of gene activity in specific pallial cell populations.
